prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen targets National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency; adverse weather causes approximately 70% of US operational delays. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s 2015 survey ranked weather-related en route delays/interruptions most significant/costly.
Elements/actors: FAA traffic managers, air traffic control system/controllers, aircraft, aircraft/flight operators, airline flight dispatchers, pilots/flight crews, general public, NASA, industry, other air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders; flight management systems and onboard weather radar.
Proposals: NASA’s Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) integrates ground-/aircraft-based technologies/decision aids to continuously seek efficient weather-avoidance routes and rapidly respond to weather/Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), supporting en route/arrival metering. Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), a cruise-focused subset, uses existing weather, airspace, traffic data, ATM automation, navigation/surveillance/communication/digital networks; targets time/fuel/cost/environmental savings.
Interactions: TMIs divert aircraft around weather and meter demand exceeding safe-separation capacity. Managers designate forecast convection regions as Flow Constrained Area (FCA), potentially implementing Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), alias Playbook routes, identified 2–8 hours before predicted constraints. Static rerouting prioritizes weather avoidance, controller workload, then efficiency. Forecast uncertainty/adjacent-sector capacity encourage conservative routes; inflight changes require substantial coordination. Current automation neither flags expired constraints nor identifies workable time/fuel-saving corrections. Controllers, dispatchers, pilots manually identify/request/amend routes, but workload prolongs unnecessary diversions.
Requirement: Dispatchers must file flight plans ≥45 minutes before gate push-back; typically 1–2 hours before takeoff. During SWAP, dispatchers select applicable routes and file revised routes.
Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) lets operators file multiple routes per flight plan, reflecting departure-delay amounts/preferences; remains strategic, providing no postdeparture efficiency/flexibility/responsiveness improvement. Crews lack congestion/conflict-aware route tools; flight management systems/radar help identify efficient trajectories, but onboard radar limits convective-weather visibility.
Conditions: fair/adverse weather, SWAP active; no formal modes specified.

New part:
U0040: They often must consult either the controller or airline dispatch about alternate trajectories that will avoid large areas of adverse weather and flow restrictions, and must coordinate with the controller to ensure an alternate trajectory will not conflict with another aircraft.
U0041: Therefore, automation tools for controllers, dispatchers, and/or flight crews that can continuously monitor real-time and short-term weather forecasts, and dynamically find workable opportunities for time- and fuel-saving corrections to weather avoidance routes, have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency in both en route and terminal transition airspace. 4 DYNAMIC WEATHER ROUTES (DWR) SYSTEM DESCRIPTION Over the past several years, NASA has developed and tested a ground-based concept called Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR) to automatically identify opportunities for more efficient trajectories around convective constraints [2][3][10].
U0042: DWR is trajectory-based concept that continuously and automatically analyzes in-flight aircraft within en route airspace to find simple amendments to flight plan routes that can save significant flying time, while accounting for convective weather, traffic conflicts, airspace sector congestion, special use airspace, and FAA routing restrictions.
U0043: DWR then alerts the user to proposed route corrections and allows them to view and modify the route prior to requesting or issuing a new route clearance.
U0044: Additionally, the DWR user interface provides strong warnings if a user modifies a DWR route such that its trial trajectory conflicts with forecast weather or traffic.
U0045: Because there are various methods and degrees to which DWR could be implemented in FAA automation systems, the term “automation” as used in this paper is intended to be generic unless specified otherwise.
U0046: DWR is an extension of the Direct-To tool developed and tested at NASA from 1998 through 2001 [4], and as a result the Direct-To functionality of identifying conflict free, operationally acceptable, direct route clearances is an integral part of DWR.
U0047: Any Direct-To route that meets the minimum wind- corrected, time-savings criteria (user-definable) will appear as a DWR route correction advisory regardless of the presence of convective weather.
U0048: Although DWR is designed to address weather related inefficiencies, its underlying logic of identifying and avoiding constraints defined by polygons would enable it to be applied to non-weather related obstacles.
U0049: Doing so could result in substantial benefits in the form of fuel, emissions and controller/pilot workload savings.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
